title: IS GOD STILL DEMANDING 10% OF YOUR MONEY—OR HAVE CHRISTIANS MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY REQUIRES?
paragraphs: IS GOD STILL DEMANDING 10% OF YOUR MONEY—OR HAVE CHRISTIANS MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY REQUIRES?

The uncomfortable truth about tithing, Malachi's warning, the New Covenant, and the kind of generosity that cannot be measured by a percentage. What if the question was never simply how much you owe God—but whether He truly has your heart?
There is a Christian somewhere right now staring at the last few bills in their wallet.
The electricity bill is overdue. The refrigerator is nearly empty. Their child needs something for school. Payday is still several days away.
And Sunday is coming.
They remember what someone told them from the pulpit.
"If you don't give God His ten percent, you're robbing Him."

They remember Malachi 3:10. They remember hearing about the windows of heaven opening. They remember the warnings about financial curses and the testimonies of people who supposedly became wealthy because they faithfully tithed.
Now they're afraid.
Not because they don't love Jesus.
Not because they want to keep everything for themselves.
But because they're wondering whether feeding their children before putting ten percent into the offering plate means they're failing God.
And perhaps you've been there.

Perhaps you've given faithfully for years, yet still struggled financially. Perhaps you've felt guilty every time you couldn't reach ten percent. Or perhaps you're on the other side—financially comfortable, faithfully giving exactly ten percent, quietly assuming that means you've fulfilled your responsibility to God.
Here is the question that could unsettle both of you.
What if the New Testament never actually commands Christians to give exactly ten percent of their income to the church?
And what if discovering that truth doesn't make generosity less important—but makes it more beautiful, more sacrificial, and more deeply rooted in Jesus Christ?
Before anyone accuses this message of encouraging Christians to stop giving, understand something.
This is not an argument against supporting the church, helping ministers, caring for the poor, or financing the spread of the Gospel.
Scripture clearly teaches those responsibilities.
This is about something far more important.
We must never place a burden on someone's conscience that Jesus and His apostles did not place there.
And we must never use the fear of losing God's favor to extract money from people whom Christ purchased with His blood.
Because the Gospel is not a financial transaction.
And grace is not something you can purchase with ten percent.
To understand this properly, we need to go back—long before modern church buildings, electronic donations, and envelopes marked "Tithes and Offerings."
We need to go back to the Scriptures themselves.
The Hebrew word commonly translated as "tithe" is מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿăśēr), meaning "a tenth" or "tenth part."
That is what the word means.
A tenth.
But understanding a word's meaning is not the same as understanding whether every command involving that word applies to every believer under every covenant.
That distinction changes everything.
In Genesis 14:18–20, Abraham gives Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils following his victory in battle.
This is significant because it occurs before the Law of Moses.
Some Christians therefore argue that tithing is an eternal principle that predates the Mosaic covenant.
And there is a legitimate observation here: giving a tenth was practiced before Sinai.
But notice what the passage does not say.
It does not command Abraham to give ten percent of his regular income for the rest of his life.
It does not establish a recurring requirement for every future believer.
It describes Abraham giving a tenth of the spoils from a particular victory.
Hebrews 7:4 refers to this event and emphasizes the greatness of Melchizedek, to whom Abraham gave a tenth of the choicest spoils.
The argument in Hebrews 7 is about the superiority of Christ's priesthood—not a new command requiring Christians to pay ten percent to their pastors.
That matters.
Because we cannot turn every historical act recorded in Scripture into a universal command.
In Genesis 28:20–22, Jacob also vows to give God a tenth if God will be with him, provide for him, and bring him home in peace.
Again, the passage is important.
But it records a personal vow, not a universal command to the New Covenant church.
Then we arrive at the Law of Moses.
And here, tithing becomes part of Israel's covenant obligations.
Leviticus 27:30 says in the King James Version:
"And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land, or of the fruit of the tree, is the LORD'S: it is holy unto the LORD."
Notice the context.
The tithe concerns agricultural produce from the land.
Leviticus 27:32 also refers to the tenth animal passing under the rod from the herd or flock.
Numbers 18:21 explains that the Levites received tithes in Israel because of their service at the tabernacle.
The Levites had a special role in Israel's worship and did not receive a territorial inheritance like the other tribes.
Deuteronomy 14:22–29 describes further instructions involving tithes, worship, rejoicing before God, and provision for Levites and vulnerable people.
Deuteronomy 26:12–13 connects the third-year tithe with provision for Levites, foreigners, fatherless children, and widows.

The exact calculation and relationship of these tithes have been debated by biblical scholars. Some understand them as multiple distinct tithes, while others understand parts of the legislation differently.
But the central point is unmistakable.
Biblical tithing under Moses was embedded in Israel's covenant system of land, agriculture, priesthood, worship, and community provision.
It was not simply an identical version of a modern Christian giving ten percent of a monthly salary to a local church.
And that brings us to one of the most quoted—and frequently misunderstood—passages in the entire conversation.
Malachi 3:8–10.
"Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me."
Those words have frightened generations of Christians.
Some have heard them delivered with such intensity that they began to imagine God standing over their bank accounts, waiting to punish them for every missing percentage.
But who was Malachi addressing?
Malachi 1:1 identifies the message as the word of the Lord to Israel.
Malachi confronts serious covenant unfaithfulness, including corruption in worship and failures among the priests.
In Malachi 3:9, the warning is addressed to the nation.
And Malachi 3:10 says:
"Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house..."
The Hebrew word translated "storehouse" is אוֹצָר (ʾōṣār), a term referring to a treasury or storage place.
In this context, the storehouse was connected to the temple's provision system.
It was not originally a reference to a modern church's bank account.
Nor was Malachi writing to Gentile Christians living under the New Covenant centuries later.
God was confronting covenant violations within Israel.
Does that mean Malachi has nothing to teach Christians?
Absolutely not.
It teaches us that God takes worship, faithfulness, justice, and provision for His servants seriously.
It warns against religious hypocrisy.
It reveals the seriousness of withholding what was required under that covenant.
But applying a passage's enduring moral lessons is different from declaring that its specific covenant penalties automatically apply to Christians today.
This distinction is crucial.
Because Galatians 3:13 declares:
"Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us..."
Read that again.
Christ redeemed us.
The believer's standing before God rests on Jesus Christ, not on successful completion of a financial percentage.
That does not make greed acceptable.
It does not excuse dishonesty.
It does not eliminate the responsibility to give.
But it does mean that a Christian should not be threatened with the Mosaic covenant's curse as though Christ's redeeming work were insufficient.
And please hear this carefully.
You cannot buy your way out of a curse that Christ has already borne for you.
Now someone will ask the obvious question.
"But didn't Jesus Himself command tithing?"
Let's look at what He actually said.
In Matthew 23:23, Jesus confronts the scribes and Pharisees:
"Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith..."
He continues by saying that they should have practiced the weightier matters without neglecting the others.
So yes, Jesus affirmed the obligation of tithing for those He was addressing in that setting.
We should not pretend otherwise.
But the historical and covenant context matters.
Jesus was speaking to Jewish religious leaders operating within the Mosaic Law before His death and resurrection inaugurated the New Covenant.
His central rebuke was that meticulous religious observance had become a cover for neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
They could count tiny herbs while ignoring suffering human beings.
They could be exact about percentages and terribly wrong about the heart of God.
And that should disturb us.
Because it is possible to give ten percent faithfully while treating people cruelly.
It is possible to put money in an offering plate and still be consumed by pride, greed, bitterness, and self-righteousness.
Jesus was not impressed by religious precision without spiritual integrity.
And neither should we be.
The Greek word used for tithing in Matthew 23:23 is ἀποδεκατοῦτε (apodekatoute), meaning "you give a tenth" or "you tithe."
But Jesus' use of that word in a confrontation with Pharisees does not, by itself, establish a ten-percent command for the post-resurrection church.
The decisive question is what the apostles taught believers under the New Covenant.
And here, something remarkable happens.
When Paul gives explicit instructions about Christian giving, he does not prescribe a mandatory ten-percent minimum.
Instead, he writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
Look closely at that verse.
The Greek phrase μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης (mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs) means, in context, not out of sorrow or reluctance, nor out of compulsion or constraint.
And the expression ἱλαρὸν δότην (hilaron dotēn) describes a cheerful giver.
Paul is not saying generosity should be accidental, careless, or based only on temporary emotions.
In fact, the passage calls believers to thoughtful, deliberate generosity.
But the motivation is not coercion.
It is grace.
Not terror.
Not public embarrassment.
Not a threat that God will destroy your finances unless you meet a target.
Grace.
And in 2 Corinthians 8:12, Paul adds another essential principle:
"For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not."
According to what a person has.
Not what they do not have.
Think about the struggling parent at the beginning of this story.
The one staring at an overdue bill.
The one wondering whether God is disappointed because their children need food.
Would it be faithful to tell that parent that God will curse them unless they give away money needed for essential family care?
Paul's teaching gives us reason to reject that kind of coercion.
In 1 Timothy 5:8, he speaks strongly about the responsibility to provide for one's household.
And in 2 Corinthians 8:13, he makes clear that giving is not intended to ease others while placing the giver under crushing hardship.
This does not mean that sacrificial generosity is always comfortable.
Sometimes giving costs us deeply.
Sometimes God calls us to surrender comforts, luxuries, and personal ambitions for the sake of others.
But there is a difference between freely chosen sacrifice motivated by love and financially destructive giving extracted through spiritual intimidation.
The difference is not small.
It is the difference between shepherding people and exploiting them.
And the Bible never gives ministers permission to confuse the two.
Peter warns church leaders in 1 Peter 5:2–3 to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for dishonest gain, and not by dominating those entrusted to them.
A faithful pastor should be able to teach generosity without making poor believers afraid of God.
A faithful ministry should be able to invite financial support without suggesting that salvation, forgiveness, or divine affection can be purchased.
And a faithful Christian should be able to ask questions about church finances without being accused of rebellion.
Because biblical stewardship includes accountability on both sides.
Now perhaps you're thinking:
"So does this mean ten percent is wrong?"
No.
Not at all.
A Christian may freely choose to give ten percent as a disciplined expression of gratitude and stewardship.
For some believers, ten percent may be a helpful starting point.
For others with significant resources, ten percent may be far below what love and generosity could reasonably inspire.
And for someone experiencing severe financial hardship, a smaller amount may represent a genuine and costly sacrifice.
The New Testament does not give every Christian one identical percentage.
It gives us something more searching.
A transformed heart.
In 1 Corinthians 16:2, Paul instructs believers to set something aside regularly, in keeping with how they have prospered.
That establishes a principle of intentional and proportionate giving.
In 2 Corinthians 8–9, he encourages willing, generous, and thoughtful contributions.
In Galatians 6:6, believers are taught to share good things with those who instruct them in the Word.
In 1 Corinthians 9:13–14, Paul teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may rightly receive material support from Gospel ministry.
And in 1 Timothy 5:17–18, faithful elders who labor in preaching and teaching are recognized as worthy of support.
So let us be absolutely clear.
The absence of a mandatory New Covenant ten-percent rule does not mean the absence of a New Covenant responsibility to give.
Christians are called to support Gospel ministry.
Christians are called to help people in need.
Christians are called to share their resources.
Christians are called to resist greed.
Christians are called to generosity that reflects the character of Jesus.
But our giving is not the price of belonging to God.
It is one expression of what belonging to God does to a human heart.
And then there is the widow.
The woman whose story should make every church leader tremble before using it in a fundraising appeal.
In Mark 12:41–44, Jesus watches people putting money into the temple treasury.
Many wealthy people contribute large amounts.
Then a poor widow comes forward.
She gives two small copper coins.
Almost nothing by the world's standards.
Yet Jesus tells His disciples that she has given more than the others, because they gave from abundance while she gave out of her poverty.
It is a powerful picture.
But there is a detail we must not ignore.
Immediately before this scene, Jesus condemns scribes who "devour widows' houses" (Mark 12:40).
Immediately afterward, He foretells the temple's destruction (Mark 13:1–2).

Christians have long understood the widow's gift as an example of extraordinary sacrificial devotion. Other interpreters also emphasize the surrounding warning against a corrupt religious system that consumes the resources of vulnerable people.
These observations deserve careful consideration together.
The widow's story should never become a weapon used to pressure struggling people into giving their last money to an institution.
Jesus noticed her.
He valued what the world considered insignificant.
And He also condemned religious leaders who exploited the vulnerable.
We must not celebrate the widow's sacrifice while ignoring Christ's warning against those who devour widows' houses.
That would miss something essential about the heart of Jesus.
Perhaps the most dangerous misunderstanding in this entire debate is the idea that giving guarantees financial prosperity.
Give ten percent, and God will make you rich.
Give more, and your breakthrough will arrive faster.
Send a seed, and expect a multiplied financial harvest.
But the New Testament does not promise that every generous Christian will become wealthy.
Paul experienced hunger, hardship, and material need.
Faithful believers have suffered poverty and persecution throughout church history.
And in 1 Timothy 6:5–10, Paul warns against treating godliness as a means of financial gain and against the destructive love of money.
Second Corinthians 9 does speak about God's provision and the fruitfulness of generosity.
But the purpose is not to turn God into a mechanism for personal enrichment.
God provides so that His people may abound in good works and continue in generosity.
The ultimate harvest is not necessarily a bigger bank balance.
It includes righteousness, thanksgiving, and glory to God.
If your theology tells you that every faithful giver must become rich, what will you tell the generous believer who remains poor?
That they didn't have enough faith?
That God rejected their offering?
That they must give even more?
That is not a burden we have biblical authority to place upon them.
Jesus Christ is not a vending machine.
And the cross is not a business investment.
But now we must confront another danger.
Because some people will read all of this and immediately feel relieved.
"Good. I don't have to give anything."
And that conclusion would miss the Gospel just as seriously as legalistic tithing does.
Because the New Covenant does not free us from greed so that we can become more selfish.
It frees us to love.
Think about the early church.
Acts 2:44–45 describes believers sharing their possessions and distributing resources according to need.
Acts 4:32–35 portrays a community in which generosity helped ensure that needy believers were cared for.
These passages describe remarkable voluntary sharing, not a command that every Christian must surrender all private property.
Acts 5:4 confirms that Ananias had control over his property and the proceeds of its sale; his sin involved deception, not failure to meet a mandatory giving percentage.
Still, the generosity of the early church is breathtaking.
They understood that the Gospel had changed the way they viewed possessions.
Their money was no longer simply a tool for personal comfort.
It had become a means of serving one another.
And that is where this question becomes personal.
Not "How little can I give and still be considered obedient?"
Not "How much do I need to pay so God will bless my business?"
But something much deeper.
"Lord Jesus, everything I have comes from You. How do You want me to use what You have entrusted to me?"
That question can be uncomfortable.
Because sometimes ten percent is easier than surrender.
A person can give ten percent and still worship the remaining ninety.
A wealthy person can give ten percent without ever experiencing meaningful sacrifice.
A struggling person can give a small amount with extraordinary love.
And someone with almost nothing can honor God through generosity expressed in hospitality, service, prayer, encouragement, and faithful care for others.
Money matters.
But money is not the only measure of love.
And giving money is never a substitute for repentance, justice, mercy, or obedience.
Remember the rich young ruler in Mark 10:17–22.
Jesus did not merely tell him to calculate a tithe.
He exposed the possession that had captured his heart.
The man went away sorrowful because he had great wealth.
The problem was not that his percentage was mathematically incorrect.
The problem was that his riches had become a rival master.
And Jesus said in Matthew 6:24:
"Ye cannot serve God and mammon."
The Greek word μαμωνᾷ (mamōna) refers to wealth or riches as a master competing for devotion.
That warning applies to the rich and the poor.
A wealthy person can idolize abundance.
A struggling person can become consumed by the desperate pursuit of money.
A ministry can also fall into the temptation of treating money as its master.
That is why the church must preach both generosity and integrity.
Because when a ministry asks people to give, it carries a sacred responsibility to use those gifts faithfully.
Every offering represents someone's labor.
Someone's sacrifice.
Someone's decision to trust.
And behind some of those gifts are stories no one else can see.
A widow quietly helping others.
A worker setting aside a small amount from an exhausting paycheck.
A young believer giving from their first earnings.
These are not merely financial transactions.
They are acts of worship when offered freely in faith and love.
And they deserve to be handled with reverence.
Now we come to the heart of the matter.
The most important gift in Christianity is not the money we give God.
It is the gift God gave us.
Second Corinthians 8:9 says:
"For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich."
Paul places this truth directly inside his teaching about generosity.
The riches in view are rooted in the grace and saving work of Christ, not a universal guarantee of personal financial wealth.
Jesus gave Himself.
He entered our broken world.
He carried our sin.
He endured the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
We were spiritually bankrupt.
We could not purchase forgiveness.
We could not earn righteousness.
We could not contribute enough to erase our guilt.
But Christ paid the price we could never pay.
Not with coins.
Not with livestock.
Not with a tenth of His possessions.
With His own life.
First Peter 1:18–19 reminds believers that redemption was not accomplished with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
So when someone asks, "How much do I owe God?" the Gospel takes us somewhere deeper than arithmetic.
We owe Him our worship, our trust, our obedience, our gratitude—our very lives.
Not as payment for salvation.
But because salvation has been given to us by grace.
Romans 12:1 calls believers to present their bodies as living sacrifices to God.
That is the language of a whole life surrendered.
And a surrendered life includes our finances.
But it cannot be reduced to our finances.
Here is where I want to speak to two people.
First, to the person who has been giving faithfully for years.
Please don't hear this article as a dismissal of your sacrifice.
If you have been setting aside ten percent with joy, gratitude, and a desire to honor God, there is no reason to be ashamed of that discipline.
Keep being generous.
Keep supporting sound biblical ministry.
Keep helping those in need.
Keep asking the Lord to make your heart more like His.
But do not imagine that your percentage makes you more loved than the believer who cannot afford the same amount.
And do not look down on someone whose financial circumstances are different from yours.
Now, to the person who has been quietly afraid.
The single mother.
The unemployed father.
The student surviving on almost nothing.
The elderly believer choosing between medication and groceries.
The person whose heart wants to give but whose circumstances are painfully limited.
Please hear this.
Your poverty does not make you a second-class Christian.
Your inability to give ten percent does not mean Christ has abandoned you.
And your salvation is not suspended until your financial situation improves.
Jesus knows your circumstances.
He sees your heart.
He understands the difference between unwillingness and inability.
And the church should be a place where you can receive care, not merely a place where you are pressured to give.
The same Gospel that calls us to generosity also commands us to love our neighbors.
Sometimes that means the congregation should be helping the struggling family rather than demanding more money from them.
That is not weak Christianity.
That is biblical compassion.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to repent.
Not only those who have been selfish with their money.
But those who have used Scripture carelessly.
Those who have confused fundraising with faithfulness.
Those who have implied that financial blessing can be bought.
Those who have made struggling believers feel unwelcome because their offerings were small.
And those of us who have given faithfully while secretly becoming proud of ourselves.
There is grace for all of us at the foot of the cross.
But grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to repent.
To make things right.
To become generous without becoming boastful.
To become responsible without becoming fearful.
To give without demanding repayment from God.
To serve without turning people into financial opportunities.
And to remember that every Christian ministry, including Gospel Warrior, must remain accountable to the very Scriptures it proclaims.
That brings me to something personal about this mission.

Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim Jesus Christ, encourage biblical discipleship, strengthen struggling believers, and help people move from shame and spiritual confusion toward repentance, grace, and transformation.
Those resources are intended to help believers grow in Scripture, understand the Gospel, and walk more deeply with Jesus Christ.
And we want that work to continue reaching more people.
The exhausted believer scrolling late at night.
The person ashamed to return to church.
The father trying to rebuild his family.
The young Christian confused by competing teachings.
The person who has never truly understood why Jesus died.
This mission takes time, work, resources, and faithful support.
Not because you owe Gospel Warrior ten percent.
But because freely chosen, consistent support can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
It should never be presented as a replacement for every other biblical responsibility, nor as a compulsory payment to God.
But it can be a genuine offering of gratitude and stewardship when given freely, responsibly, and according to your means.
Please do not feel ashamed.
You can still be part of this mission.
Not simply to help an algorithm.
But because somewhere among your friends and family may be a believer who has spent years living under unnecessary guilt about tithing.
Someone may need to discover that grace does not cancel generosity—it transforms its motivation.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Because this is not just a discussion about money.
It is a discussion about what we believe God is like.
Do we see Him as a Father who loves His children through Christ?
Or as a collector waiting to punish anyone who misses a payment?
Do we give because we have received grace?
Or because we are afraid that grace might disappear?
Do we support ministries because we believe in their faithfulness to Scripture?
Or because someone has convinced us that questioning financial demands is the same as questioning God?
These are questions worth bringing into the light.
So I want to ask you something, and I hope you will answer from your heart.
Have you ever felt afraid that God would punish you financially because you could not give ten percent?
Or have you experienced the joy of giving freely, without fear, because you understood what Christ has already done for you?
And if you believe Christians should still be required to tithe ten percent, you are welcome in this conversation too. Share the Scriptures that have shaped your conviction.
Let us reason together respectfully, test our conclusions against the whole counsel of God, and refuse to make enemies out of fellow believers who are sincerely trying to honor Christ.
Because the goal is not to win an argument about money.
The goal is to know Jesus more faithfully.
To obey His Word more carefully.
To become more generous.
More compassionate.
More honest.
More surrendered.
And more like the Savior who gave Himself for us.
So, is tithing ten percent still a requirement for Christians under the New Covenant?

The strongest reading of the New Testament is that Christians are not placed under a universal, mandatory ten-percent tithe. Instead, believers are instructed to give willingly, intentionally, proportionately, generously, and in love.

Faithful Christians differ on this issue. Some teach ten percent as a continuing obligation or normative minimum, drawing on Abraham, the Mosaic tithe, and Jesus' words about tithing. Others understand the tithe as a covenant-specific command fulfilled in Christ, while affirming the New Testament's strong commands concerning generosity and material support.
Those differences should be acknowledged honestly.

But what is clear is that the New Testament does not present a simple formula in which paying ten percent purchases God's favor, guarantees prosperity, or determines whether someone belongs to Christ.
And that truth should change the way we speak about giving.
Ten percent may be a useful personal discipline.
It is not the price of grace.
Giving is an act of worship.
It is not a substitute for obedience.
Supporting Gospel ministry is a biblical responsibility.
It is not permission for ministries to manipulate people.
And financial generosity should flow from love for Christ, not terror of losing His affection.
So perhaps the question we should carry away from this conversation is not simply, "Have I given God His ten percent?"
Perhaps it is:
"Jesus, now that I know what You have given for me, how can I faithfully honor You with everything You have entrusted to my care?"
That question reaches beyond the offering plate.
Into our homes.
Our spending.
Our savings.
Our debts.
Our generosity.
Our treatment of the poor.
Our support for faithful Gospel work.
And the quiet places of our hearts where money sometimes competes with God.
If you have been selfish, there is room to repent.
If you have been fearful, there is room to rediscover grace.
If you have been manipulated, there is room to seek truth and healing.
If you have been generous, there is room to grow still more.
And if you have been trying to earn God's love through your giving, hear the Gospel one more time.
Christ did not wait for you to become financially worthy before He went to the cross.
He loved us while we were still sinners.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives salvation by grace, not by financial achievement.
That is where true Christian generosity begins.
Not with a calculator.
Not with a threat.
Not with an envelope.
But with a crucified and risen Savior.
And when that truth finally settles into the deepest part of your heart, you begin to understand something unforgettable.
Jesus never asked you to purchase the grace He already paid for with His blood.
